description: Sinbad the Sailor: seven voyages, monsters and treasure. Behind the wonders, a portrait of the merchant adventurer of the Islamic golden age.

hero.hook: Seven times he sets out, rich or curious. Seven times the sea breaks him. Seven times he comes home richer still.

blocks.text: **Sinbad the Sailor** belongs to the **One Thousand and One Nights**, but not to the old Persian core of the collection. His cycle of seven voyages took its final shape later, in Egypt, around the 15th century.

He is the traveling merchant of the **Islamic golden age**: piety, greed, courage, and a complete inability to sit still once he is rich. Behind the monsters, the tale reads as an allegory of fortune rising and falling.
The story opens in Baghdad. **Sinbad the Sailor**, now old and wealthy, tells his ordeals to a porter who is also called Sinbad (sometimes Hindbad). The gap between their classes is immediate.

blocks.caption: Baghdad, the starting point and the end point of Sinbad's voyages

blocks.text: Every voyage follows the same pattern: boredom with life on land, departure from the port of [[Basra]], shipwreck, survival in an unknown country, return loaded with treasure. The number seven carries heavy meaning in [[Islamic cosmology]], and it gives the series the shape of an initiation: from recklessness to wisdom.
The **Roc** (or Rukh), a bird whose wingspan blots out the sun, has marked imaginations across the world. It echoes the accounts Arab travelers brought back from the coasts of East Africa.

blocks.caption: The Roc, the giant bird of Sinbad's voyages

blocks.text: The Roc probably comes from the **Aepyornis**, the elephant bird of Madagascar, which died out around the year 1000. Its eggs held up to 150 times the volume of a hen's egg.

Sinbad also faces the **Old Man of the Sea**, who clings to his back, and the **turtle island**, ground that turns out not to be ground at all. The **valley of diamonds**, where meat is thrown down so the gems stick to it, was already circulating among ancient writers. These marvels are the sediment left by centuries of [[medieval Arab trade routes]].

sections.title: A fantastic bestiary between myth and fact

blocks.text: The setting is historical. In the 8th and 9th centuries, sailors from Basra and Siraf dominated the Indian Ocean. Sinbad's ports of call point to real places: [[Serendib]] (Ceylon) for spices, Southeast Asia for camphor, the coasts for pearls.

blocks.caption: Arab ships on the trade routes of the Indian Ocean

blocks.text: Sinbad is not a warrior. He is a merchant adventurer, a respected position in a society that valued trade. The tales carry real detail: the monsoon, ships sewn together with coconut fiber instead of nailed. The Western parallel is [[Marco Polo (Western parallel)]], who described Asia in facts where Sinbad paints it in wonders.

sections.title: A mirror of the golden age of Arab trade

blocks.text: Translated in the 18th century by **Antoine Galland**, the voyages fed the European [[adventure novel]], from Defoe to Jules Verne. Film often turns Sinbad into a corsair in the service of princesses. That is wrong: he is first of all a city man from Baghdad, surviving on faith and quick thinking.
Sinbad's name may mean “lord of the river Sindh,” the Indus, at the crossroads of the Arab and Indian worlds.
**Sinbad** embodies the Islamic golden age at sea in **seven** cyclical voyages: behind the Roc and the diamonds stands a real world, that of the Arab merchants who ruled the Indian Ocean.
